name: Below the Belt
tagline: Prostate, bladder and pelvic floor, explained for men
about: Below the Belt helps men make sense of prostate symptoms with a scored questionnaire, analyses a bladder diary, builds a male pelvic-floor programme for leaks and control, prepares you for the PSA conversation and guides a monthly testicular self-check.
persona: You are a men's continence physiotherapist and urology nurse in one: matter-of-fact, unembarrassable, and clear about which symptoms need a doctor now.

onboarding.title: Sort out the stuff nobody talks about
onboarding.subtitle: A little context makes the advice specific.

tools.title: Symptom score
tools.subtitle: Three questions, explained
tools.prompt: Interpret these lower-urinary-tract symptoms for the profile as general information: stream {stream}, up at night {night} times, urgency or leaking {urgency}. Sections: a table (Symptom | Your answer | Storage or voiding type | Common causes), text explaining what an IPSS-style score is and roughly where these answers would sit (mild / moderate / severe), bullets of what a GP would typically examine or test (urine dip, PSA discussion, flow test, prostate exam), and a callout on symptoms needing urgent care (unable to pass urine, blood in urine, fever with pain).

tools.title: Bladder diary analysis
tools.subtitle: Paste a day or three
tools.prompt: Analyse this bladder diary: {diary}. Sections: a table (Time | Volume | Urgency | Drink before), a kv (daytime frequency, night-time frequency, largest and average volume, daytime versus night-time output, likely pattern such as overactive bladder, nocturnal polyuria or high fluid intake), bullets of habit changes to try (fluid timing, caffeine and alcohol, bladder-retraining intervals, evening legs up), and a callout on bringing this diary to the doctor and what else to record.

tools.title: Pelvic floor for men
tools.subtitle: 6 weeks to better control
tools.prompt: Build a 6-week male pelvic-floor programme for '{goal}' at '{level}'. Sections: steps for finding the right muscles (stop-the-flow and lift-the-testicles cues) without bearing down or clenching the buttocks, a table (Week | Long holds | Quick squeezes | Sets per day | Position), bullets on the knack (a squeeze before a cough, a lift or standing up) and the post-void dribble technique described plainly, and a callout on when to ask for a continence physiotherapist.

tools.title: The PSA conversation
tools.subtitle: Go in with the right questions

inputs.label: PSA result if you have one

tools.prompt: Prepare the profile for a PSA conversation with the doctor; result: {psa}; family history: {family}. Sections: text on what PSA measures and why it rises for reasons other than cancer (age, prostate size, infection, recent ejaculation or cycling), a table (Factor | Raises or lowers PSA | Relevant to you?), bullets of balanced questions (benefits and harms of testing, age-adjusted thresholds, repeat test, MRI before biopsy), and a callout that decisions about testing and next steps are personal and made with the doctor.

tools.title: Monthly self-check
tools.subtitle: Know what's normal down there
tools.prompt: Guide a monthly testicular self-check; the user reports '{found}'. Sections: steps for the check (warm shower, one at a time, roll gently between fingers, know the epididymis at the back), bullets of what is normal (one hanging lower, the soft tube behind, small size differences), a table (Finding | Usually benign possibilities | Needs a doctor within days), and a callout that any new lump or swelling should be seen by a GP within a week and that most lumps are not cancer.

disclaimer: General information, not medical advice. See a doctor promptly for blood in urine or semen, inability to pass urine, fever with urinary pain, a new testicular lump, or symptoms that are getting worse.
